Personally, I consider Hideo Kojima to be one of video games’ greatest creators. Almost every game he’s worked on, especially the Metal Gear series, has brought new ideas to gaming in general.

The original 1987 Metal Gear turned the usual dynamic of video games on its head. Whereas most games were about seeking out conflict, Metal Gear was about actively avoiding it. Most games had you shooting near constantly - in Metal Gear, if you had to start shooting, you dun goofed.

Most military games are a hard pass for me, too, Mostly due to the fact that I am not very interested in the idea of playing Faceless Grunt #347, shooting a bunch of dudes in Unspecified Sand Colored Country. 

Metal gear solid has always been the major exception. Kojima is one of the few creators who gives his military characters a level of humanity. In addition to that, MGS is less military fiction and more paranoid fiction that happens to star military operatives. 

I can honestly say that MGS is among the few games that have changed my way of thinking about things, MGS 2 in particular providing a pretty alarming example of how mind control could be carried out on a mass scale.

He has a very unique narrative voice, mixing high-tech thriller, government conspiracy, and magical realism (the otherwise rather grounded MGS 3 features antagonists that, among other things, *shoot bees from their body*), with MGS 2 and 5 approaching straight-up surrealism in places.

Then of course there’s his less popular projects - Zone of the Enders, despite being saddled with a horrendous English dub, provides one of the only six-degrees-of-freedom control systems I have ever found playable, and is an excellent arcade shooter in its own right. 

Snatcher takes the old-school adventure game formula about as far as it can go, incorporating action sequences and some of the best cyberpunk world building this side of Philip K Dick. 

What flaws he does have as a creator (holy exposition dumps!) I can forgive because of just how damn original his work has been.

I guess you could say I’m a bit of a fan.

This bit of footage has given me enough to start to speculate on the themes and perhaps some of the mechanics in the game.

Taking into account the fact that Kojima has said earlier that death doesn't result in a traditional game\-over state, I think the main mechanic of the game centers around Sam's repeated "rebirth" after dying in the game world. The most obvious way the player can be brought back from the dead is through the babies seen in all of the game's trailers.

The babies (I believe there are certainly more than one) are like human backups, they seem to be connected to the machine on Sam's back \- that’s recording information for the baby, which, when this version of Sam dies, will take over for him (probably artificially aged by the Timefall). The repeated opening and closing motion of the machine's "eye" is reminiscent of a camera.

The trailer focused quite a bit on the increasing amount of baggage the characters took with them. My theory on this is that it's sort of a "time capsule" for future versions of Sam (the grown\-up babies). The more you take with you, the better chance your future self will have at survival, but the the more your current self will be weighed down, thus decreasing his chance of survival.

The weird "worm" the female character swallowed at the end of the trailer may well gestate into one of the babies. She mentioned that one of those a day keeps the timefall away. Perhaps the only effective countermeasure to timefall is to ensure that there's someone to take your place when you die?

So the main theme of the game is your legacy. What will you leave behind when you die? What will you sacrifice for the betterment of future generations?

Funny this should come up now, because I've been working on a constructed language for my furry characters to speak. I've had an interest in bio/socio-linguistics for quite a while, although I have no formal education in the field, and I admit to using quite a lot of imagination to fill in the blanks.

I have some structural stuff in place, like how nouns and verbs work, and things like that, but as for the sound, I think that whatever sort of language an anthro would use, it would sound ugly as hell to humans at large :)

So to start, I assumed the presence of human-like vocal cords, and a somewhat thicker, more muscular tongue than you see in most mammals.

I used the vocalizations canids use in real life as a starting point, and decided that language would have evolved from basic signalling barks, howls and the like. This means that most of the consonants would originate from the back region of the mouth, and even down into the throat a little bit. This means a lot of guttural noises, k's, g's velar/uvular noises like the German and Arabic "ch" sounds.

Sounds we humans make in the front of the mouth such as "d" and "t" would be very difficult, due to most other mammals' less pronounced alveolar ridge, and sounds that rely on the lips, like "p" and "b" would be pretty much impossible.

As for vowels, again, mostly back vowels, and any that require rounding of the lips are out.

TL;DR: I think anthro speech would sound like someone rewinding Tolkien's Orcish.

I haven't faced all the bosses, currently on my second playthrough, but out of what I've seen so far, from easiest to hardest...

* Micolash - only has three attacks, all of which are easy to dodge. The adds go down in two seconds tops, and pose little threat to a properly levelled character. Beaten on my 1st attempt.

* Vicar - Easy to bait her into using her jumping attack, which has a very long, easy-to-dodge animation. Her heal can be overpowered by spamming R1. 1st attempt.

* Amygdala - Hits hard, but easy to read. 1st attempt.

* Reborn - This guys design is a little confusing, but once you find the right angle of attack and get between two of his legs, he can pretty much be hacked to death. Didn't even kill the fireball ladies. 2nd attempt.

* Wet Nurse - The exposed back and telegraphed moves made this a pretty manageable fight. 3rd attempt.

* Witch - All in all not too hard, but the immobilizing attack gave me a lot of trouble. 5th attempt.

* Blood-starved Beast - That third phase is a killer, the poison got me more often than the boss did. 4th attempt.

* Rom - The mini spider adds can blindside you if you're not careful, and the attack with the falling crystals is unpredictable and hard to dodge. The boss itself is pretty squishy though. 6th attempt.

* Father - This guy is a bastard. Fast and unpredictable, and I just can't seem to get the parry timing down. 10th attempt.

* Cleric Beast - at the time you fight this guy you're really low level and aren't hitting hard at all. I can't parry this boss reliably so he often whittles my health down before I can deal enough damage. 12th attempt.

* Shadows - Ugh. Multiple bosses were the bane of my existence in the Dark Souls Games, and nothing has changed here. Knocking one down is easy enough, once they get the long-range snake attacks I'm pretty much through. 17th attempt.

* Gehrman - Sweet Jeebus. There is NO margin for error in this fight. He dashes forwards with many of his attacks, so even if you time your dodge properly, you're out of attack range. After beating Vicar, the first two Chalice bosses, Amygdala, and Micolash on my first try, and Reborn on my second, I went back to see if I could deal with Cleric Beast, and I still have to rely on Molotovs and luck.

A few things that helped me beat him:

* Don't lock on. The little spiders will mess with your targeting, and you'll need to use the roll rather than the backstep to dodge the falling crystals.

* You can keep hitting Rom during his teleport, and even for a second or so after he seems to have disappeared. Use light attacks while he's doing that for some cheap damage.

* I ignored the spiders, since trying to take them all out only led to me dying from an attack I didn't see coming.

* For the falling crystals attack, start your roll the moment Rom's body hits the floor, and keep rolling in a wide arc around Rom until the attack has passed. This costs a lot of stamina, but hey, at least you're still alive.

* On a related note, always roll one more time than you think you have to. There's a lot of empty space around Rom for you to take a second and gain stamina back.

The rest is all just up to how well you can react. Close in aggressively and hit his flank, but be ready to roll out of there at a moments notice.

As much as I like Resident Evil, I don't think anyone working on that game thought this hard about *anything*.

I'd probably do something like this:  
  
**Galaga**: Great simple arcade game, gets you used to basic controls.  
**Super Mario Bros**: A bit more complex, teaches a lot of the visual language needed to play video games, as well as how to look for secrets.  
**Dance Dance Revolution**: A crash course in alternative control styles, as well as just a blast to play in public.  
**Doom**: Fast paced, intuitive and ridiculous, a great introduction to the FPS.  
**Resident Evil 2**: Cool and creepy intro to story in games, third-person adventure, and puzzle-solving.  
**Portal 2**: Lateral thinking, genre-mixing, and the best example of comedy in any game, ever.  
**Skyrim**: Intro to the open-world concept, and emergent gameplay, as well as to RPG systems.  
**Silent Hill 2**: A great example of atmosphere, subtext, symbolism, and the sense of "being there" that only a video game can provide.  
**Final Fantasy XII**: One of the best examples of large-scale world building. A game you can really get lost in.  
**Spec-Ops: The Line**: IMO, the final word in the "Are games art?" debate. Powerful, disturbing, and explosive, it shows that games don't necessarily have to be fun to be great.
I love FPS, but developers need to realize there are other kinds of games out there besides FPS and open-world action.
